query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the effective in-flight particle velocity by extending the spray distance (to about 300–350 mm) for the HVAF-i7 torch will improve deposition efficiency and overcome the thickness limitation for FeCoNiCrAl bond coats.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powder with 15–45 μm feedstock as used in HVAF-M3 processing
generation.intervention: Adjust the HVAF-i7 process by extending the stand-off (spray) distance to around 300–350 mm to achieve higher particle velocities
generation.conditions: Deposition using the HVAF-i7 torch on substrates (including in internal diameters as small as 120 mm) intended for high-temperature thermal-barrier service, with the same 15–45 μm feedstock
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced kinetic energy of the spray particles which promotes better splat formation and deposit buildup, while moderating in-flight oxidation
generation.mechanism: A longer spray distance permits acceleration of the powder particles to higher velocities before impingement. This increased kinetic energy improves the impact-induced flattening and adhesion of the particles on the substrate, thereby increasing the deposition rate and resulting in a thicker, well-adherent bond coat with minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline (coatings deposited with the standard HVAF-i7 parameters using 15–45 μm feedstock), the intervention should yield a thicker bond coat that maintains high-quality adhesion and oxidation resistance during elevated-temperature service.
generation.baseline: Coatings produced by HVAF-M3 with 15–45 μm feedstock, which have optimal quality but can be applied in larger internal diameters, while the HVAF-i7 using the same parameters yields acceptable quality but inadequate thickness
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective as long as the increased spray distance does not lead to excessive cooling or unwanted particle oxidation. Its benefit may be limited if changes in spray dynamics adversely affect the coating microstructure or bonding when depositing inside small-diameter (120 mm) components.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether the increased in-flight time at longer stand-off distances might introduce a critical level of oxidation or cause other microstructural alterations. Fine-tuning of the spray parameters may be required to maintain the desired coating integrity in all service conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a series of HVAF-i7 deposition experiments in which the spray distance is varied from the default setting to 300 mm and 350 mm, while keeping all other parameters and the 15–45 μm feedstock constant. Measure deposition efficiency, coating thickness, oxidation levels, and adhesion strength on substrates with internal diameters as small as 120 mm.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If extending the spray distance to 300–350 mm does not produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness or if it leads to degradation in adhesion quality or unacceptable increases in oxidation, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.

As reported in [,,,], HVOF as-sprayed AlTiCrFeCoNi coatings possessed a dense microstructure and a high microhardness over 750 HV with a good fracture toughness. The heat-treated NiCoFeCrSiAlTi coating exhibits a hardness even higher than 800 HV, good wear resistance, and oxidation resistance at 1100 °C, similar to that of MCrAlY coating []. The cavitation erosion resistance of the AlCoCrFeNi coating is about 3.5 times that of 06Cr13Ni5Mo steel in the same environment []. The high wear resistance of AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA at elevated temperatures is associated with oxidation behavior. The formation of a compact oxide layer on the AlCoCrFeNi and AlTiCrFeCoNi HVOF coatings accounts for enhanced wear resistance at temperatures ≥ 800 °C [] and a lowered coefficient of friction due to its function as a solid lubricant []. In [], it was found that additions of Nd and Mo to a AlCrFeCoNi base significantly reduced the wear depth at increasing temperatures due to improved oxide layer adhesion. Thus, AlCoCrFeNiMo coatings deposited using HVOF are suitable for high-temperature application.
